name: Eval — HN CLI end-to-end
description: 4-stage evaluation workflow: plan → code → test → review-with-approval. Builds a small Node CLI that fetches the Hacker News top stories API and renders them.

variables.name: moduleName
variables.label: Module name
variables.description: Kebab-case module name; used as file prefix.

variables.name: storyCount
variables.label: Number of stories to fetch
variables.description: How many top stories the CLI should render.

variables.name: apiUrl
variables.label: HN Firebase API base URL
variables.description: Base URL for Hacker News API.

stages.name: 1-plan
stages.description: Produce a design plan for the CLI without writing code.

prompts.label: plan
prompts.text:
You are a senior TypeScript engineer designing a small Node.js CLI named `{{moduleName}}`.

Goal: The CLI fetches the top {{storyCount}} stories from the Hacker News Firebase API at `{{apiUrl}}` and prints them to the terminal in a readable, colored format.

Produce a concise MARKDOWN design plan that includes:
1. File layout — every file you will create with a one-line description each (source files, test files, package.json fields, config).
2. Public API — function signatures for each module (`src/{{moduleName}}.ts`, `src/api.ts`, `src/render.ts`, `bin/{{moduleName}}.ts` or equivalent). Include TypeScript types.
3. Runtime flow — a numbered sequence from CLI entry to final rendered output.
4. Error handling — network failures, missing IDs, non-200 responses, empty story list, malformed JSON.
5. External libraries — pick minimal, pure-ESM libraries (justify each). Use `undici` or built-in `fetch` for HTTP; `picocolors` for colors; `vitest` for tests. No frameworks.
6. Test strategy — what will be unit-tested vs. integration-tested; how HTTP is mocked.
7. Edge cases explicitly considered.

Do NOT write code yet. Do NOT invoke any file-editing tools. Reply with markdown only. Keep the whole plan under 600 words.

stages.name: 2-code
stages.description: Implement the CLI following the plan; write real files.

prompts.label: code
prompts.text:
Implement the plan from the previous stage. Create the following ACTUAL files in the working directory using your file-editing tools (Write/Create/Edit). Do NOT paste file contents in a markdown code block — you must actually write them to disk.

Required files (relative paths):
- `package.json` — module type=ESM, `bin` field pointing to the CLI entry, minimal deps (undici OR node built-in fetch — pick built-in `fetch` since Node 18+), `picocolors` for coloring. Include a `scripts.test` running vitest.
- `tsconfig.json` — strict, moduleResolution NodeNext, target ES2022, outDir dist.
- `src/api.ts` — exports `fetchTopStoryIds(limit: number, baseUrl: string): Promise<number[]>` and `fetchStory(id: number, baseUrl: string): Promise<Story>`, with a `Story` type. Use `fetch`.
- `src/render.ts` — exports `renderStory(story: Story, rank: number): string` and `renderStories(stories: Story[]): string`. Use picocolors.
- `src/{{moduleName}}.ts` — exports `run(count: number, baseUrl: string): Promise<string>`; orchestrates api + render.
- `bin/{{moduleName}}.ts` — CLI entry with shebang; parses argv for `--count` / `-n` (default {{storyCount}}) and `--url` (default `{{apiUrl}}`); calls `run` and prints result. Exit code 1 on error.
- `README.md` — one-paragraph description + install/run/test example.

Hard requirements:
- All source under `src/` and `bin/` — no code outside those directories.
- Pure ESM (`"type": "module"` in package.json, `.js` extensions in relative imports from `.ts` sources per NodeNext).
- Handle non-200 responses and network errors gracefully (throw a typed `HnApiError`).
- Rank numbers 1..N, not 0..N-1.
- No `any`. No `as` unless truly unavoidable.

After writing the files, reply with a brief summary listing every file you created and one sentence on how the pieces connect. Keep the reply under 200 words.

stages.name: 3-tests
stages.description: Write unit tests + a mocked integration test for the CLI. Run them to confirm they pass.

prompts.label: tests
prompts.text:
Add tests for the CLI created in the previous stage. Write real files with your file-editing tools.

Required test files (relative paths):
- `tests/api.test.ts` — unit tests for `fetchTopStoryIds` and `fetchStory`. Mock `global.fetch` (vi.stubGlobal). Cover: happy path with N ids returned; slicing to `limit`; non-200 response throws `HnApiError`; malformed JSON throws.
- `tests/render.test.ts` — unit tests for `renderStory` / `renderStories`. Verify rank prefix, title present, url present when defined, ansi stripping (use `strip-ansi` or a simple regex) to make assertions stable across environments.
- `tests/cli.test.ts` — integration-ish test that imports `run()`, stubs `fetch`, and asserts the returned string contains {{storyCount}} numbered lines.
- `vitest.config.ts` — minimal config with `test.environment='node'`.

Hard requirements:
- Use vitest. No jest imports.
- Strip ANSI in assertions so tests don't break when color is toggled.
- Cover the error paths, not just happy paths.

Then run `pnpm test` (or `npm test`) in the working directory via your Shell tool and paste the output in your reply. If tests fail, fix them and re-run until they pass. Reply with the final passing test output plus a one-paragraph explanation of what is covered.

stages.name: 4-review
stages.description: Human review gate. Reviewer must approve or send feedback.

prompts.label: review
prompts.text:
You are the code-review agent. The previous stages produced a CLI plus tests. Read every file in the working directory (use your file-reading tools) and produce a REVIEW REPORT in markdown covering:

1. Summary (2-3 sentences) — did the implementation match the plan?
2. Correctness — for each source file, one bullet: bug / risk / OK.
3. Test quality — coverage of edge cases, mock realism, false negatives.
4. TypeScript hygiene — strictness, any-uses, unnecessary casts.
5. UX — CLI ergonomics, error messages, exit codes.
6. Suggested follow-ups (max 5, prioritized).

Be honest and unbiased. Do NOT rewrite code in this stage — call out issues only.

After your review, wait for approval. The human reviewer will either approve (advance) or send feedback (which you must then act on as a follow-up prompt).
